What the f*ck is ARCHVE?

ARCHVE is aiming to document Art, Records, Culture, Humanity, Visions & Expression from people all over the world. We believe theres already so much media based around big people, and big stories going on in the world, but, there's so much more out there that just simply isn't being documented.

ARCHVE is a magazine—but that answer feels too small.

It is a public archive for the people, ideas, images, sounds, and stories that deserve to exist somewhere permanent. It is a place for discovery, creative experimentation, and genuine human expression. Most importantly, it is the print magazine I have always dreamed of creating.

For as long as I can remember, I have wanted a platform where I could showcase cool people doing cool things. Music, art, fashion, film, spirituality, personal stories, strange ideas, obscure interests—anything created or experienced with enough passion to make someone else stop and pay attention.

“Cool” does not have to mean famous. It does not have to mean profitable, verified, connected, or approved by an industry. Sometimes the coolest person in the world is creating alone in a bedroom, working a regular job, living in a city nobody pays attention to, and making something incredible without an audience.

That person still deserves to be documented.

The problem is that much of modern media is structured around status. The same major artists, celebrities, companies, and cultural moments are discussed repeatedly because attention has already validated them. Publications cover what is guaranteed to generate traffic, and algorithms continue circulating the names people already recognize.

Meanwhile, an entire world of human creativity remains invisible.

There are people everywhere with unbelievable stories, rare talents, unconventional perspectives, and fully developed ideas who may never receive meaningful coverage. Not because their work lacks value, but because they do not have enough followers, industry connections, social credibility, or money to make traditional media acknowledge them.

ARCHVE is being created to challenge that system.

I want this to be one of the few media platforms where access is not determined by popularity. It should never feel like an exclusive club or a pay-to-play publication where recognition is reserved for whoever can afford it. Anyone should be able to submit an image, video, story, piece of music, unfinished idea, or personal obsession and know that it will be considered for what it actually is—not dismissed because of who did or did not create it.

Talent exists before recognition. A story matters before the person telling it becomes famous.

ARCHVE should be the place that understands that.

The goal is not simply to feature people. It is to give them a meaningful piece of media they can carry forward—something that introduces their work to a new audience, strengthens their presence online, and creates a permanent record proving that their ideas existed.

There is already enough noise on the internet. ARCHVE is supposed to create focus.

When someone enters this world, I want them to encounter ideas they would not have found through an algorithm. I want them to discover a musician from a city they have never visited, read the story of someone they would have otherwise passed on the street, or become fascinated by an interest they had never considered. The platform should feel unpredictable but intentional: a place where completely different people can exist beside one another because they share the same underlying quality—something worth documenting.

I AM A DESIGNER.

Not to sound cocky, but I genuinely believe in my abilities. I understand layout, typography, color theory, image-making, photo manipulation, composition, and the emotional power of visual communication. Design is not simply something I do when I am hired. I regularly spend more than 12 hours a day creating, even when there is no immediate return, because I honestly love the process that much.

ARCHVE gives that obsession a purpose.

I want people to send me their photographs, stories, music, films, memories, and unfinished ideas so I can sit in my room and build worlds around them. I want to take raw material from another person’s life and transform it into a composition that feels considered, beautiful, and completely specific to them.

Every story should have its own visual identity. Every article should feel like an art piece. Every physical issue should be something people want to keep instead of something they skim once and throw away.

A musician should not receive the same predictable layout as a filmmaker. A deeply personal story should not be flattened into the same template as a fashion editorial. The design should respond to the subject—their personality, environment, history, and creative language. If someone trusts ARCHVE with their story, it should be treated with care.

That is the difference between filling pages and building an archive.

Right now, ARCHVE is barely getting started. At this stage, I am the founder, writer, designer, editor, creative director, web developer, and almost everything else the magazine needs. I know that will not always be the case.

My larger dream is to build ARCHVE into a company capable of employing hundreds of creative people: writers, editors, designers, photographers, filmmakers, researchers, interviewers, developers, culture scouts, and people whose future roles may not even have names yet.

I want to create the kind of company I have always wanted to work for—one that respects creative labor and actually pays artists fairly. Too many businesses depend on the passion of creative people while treating that passion as an excuse to underpay them. ARCHVE cannot claim to protect creativity while exploiting the people responsible for it.

The company must grow without abandoning the values that made it necessary.

ARCHVE will not be defined by how famous its subjects are. It will be defined by how deeply it sees them. It will not document culture from above. It will grow from within it, alongside the people actively creating it.

So, what the f*ck is ARCHVE?

It is a magazine for people who have something real to share.

It is a creative platform without a velvet rope.

It is a physical record of ideas that might otherwise disappear.

It is proof that an unknown person’s story can be treated with the same care, imagination, and importance as the biggest name in the world.

It is still becoming—and that is what makes this the perfect time to begin documenting it.
